chapters.title: Christ magnified in life or death

parts.text: Paul thanks God joyfully for the Philippians’ partnership in the gospel, confident that God will complete his work in them. He prays for discerning love and fruitful righteousness. His imprisonment has advanced the gospel, making his allegiance to Christ widely known and emboldening others to preach. Some preach from rivalry and others from love, but Paul rejoices that Christ is proclaimed.

Paul desires Christ to be magnified whether he lives or dies. Living means service for Christ; departing to be with him is far better, yet remaining would benefit the believers. He expects to continue helping their progress and joy. Regardless of whether he visits, they must live worthily of the gospel, standing united and fearless before opponents. Both faith and suffering for Christ have been granted to them, and they share the struggle they have seen in Paul.

chapters.title: The humility of Christ and faithful service

parts.text: Paul calls for unity, humility, and concern for others rather than rivalry or empty glory. Christ provides the pattern: though in God’s form and equal with God, he took a servant’s form, became human, and humbled himself to death on the cross. God has exalted him so every knee will bow and every tongue confess his lordship. Believers must work out their salvation seriously because God works within them, avoiding complaining and holding forth the word of life as lights in a crooked world.

Paul hopes to send Timotheus, whose sincere concern and proven gospel service he commends. He also sends Epaphroditus, their messenger and his fellow worker, who nearly died while serving. God mercifully restored him, and Paul asks the church to welcome and honor him with joy. His costly service supplied their help to Paul and exemplified devotion to Christ’s work.

Paul warns against teachers who place confidence in outward fleshly distinctions. He himself could claim strong credentials: circumcision, Israelite ancestry, Pharisaic standing, zeal, and legal righteousness. Yet he counts these gains as loss beside knowing Christ. He seeks righteousness from God by faith rather than his own through law, and longs to know Christ, the power of his resurrection, fellowship in his sufferings, and conformity to his death.

Paul does not claim to have arrived at perfection. Forgetting what lies behind, he presses toward God’s upward calling in Christ and urges believers to share that pursuit. They should follow faithful examples instead of enemies of the cross whose appetites and earthly interests lead to destruction. Their citizenship belongs in heaven, from which they await Jesus Christ. He will transform their lowly bodies to resemble his glorious body by the power that subjects everything to him.

Paul urges steadfastness and reconciliation between Euodias and Syntyche, asking help for these fellow workers. Believers should rejoice in the Lord, show gentleness, and bring every concern to God with thanksgiving instead of anxiety. God’s surpassing peace will guard their hearts and minds in Christ. Paul directs their thoughts toward what is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, commendable, and worthy of praise, and calls them to practice what they learned from him.

Paul rejoices in their renewed support, while explaining that he has learned contentment in hunger or plenty through Christ’s strength. Their repeated gifts are welcome partnership in his affliction and a pleasing offering to God. He seeks fruit credited to them, not merely gifts for himself, and assures them that God will supply their needs. He closes with greetings, including from Cesar’s household, and Christ’s grace.
